extracted.intended_audience: maritime historians, sailing enthusiasts, and students of nautical history
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and practical principles for evaluating the performance, handling, and commercial suitability of late‑19th/early‑20th century sailing clippers on long passages (especially to Australia/New Zealand). Includes metrics, ship design and rigging effects, seamanship, cargo stowage, and logging practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voyage duration and waypoint timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure passage performance by total days out and by timing at key waypoints (dates of departure, crossing the Equator, passing the Cape meridian, passing the Otway, and date arrived).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text repeatedly tabulates departures, dates at equator/Cape meridian/Otway and arrival dates (e.g., Cutty Sark: crossed line 23 April, Cape meridian 26 May, passed Otway 18 June, arrived 21 June — 80 days out). Use these milestones to verify and compare passage claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: 24‑hour run (daily run) as short‑term performance metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Record and evaluate a ship's daily mileage runs (24‑hour runs) to characterise short‑term performance and streaks of high speed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Loch Carron made three consecutive 24‑hour runs of 310, 320 and 332 miles; Loch Broom ran 301 miles in 24 hours on one day and 282 the next. Use best 24‑hour runs to compare capabilities and to detect periods of advantageous weather or exceptional performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Head‑to‑head races and seasonal bests
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare ships by direct races (ships sailing in company or the same season) and by 'race of the year' results to determine relative speed and consistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Cutty Sark, Samuel Plimsoll, Sir Walter Raleigh and City of York race is cited as deciding the season's fastest. Use contemporaneous races and reports to validate claims rather than isolated single passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ship sail plan versus carrying power trade‑off
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess how sail plan geometry and carrying capacity interact: narrow sail plans with greater carrying power often reduce top speed compared with finer, lighter sailers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Torridon and Yallaroi had narrow sail plans and, despite greater carrying power, were not as fast as Cimba or Romanoff. Evaluate vessel role (speed vs cargo) when judging performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hull stiffness/tenderness and handling characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate a vessel's 'stiffness' or 'tenderness' (initial stability) because it affects handling, safety in heavy weather, and what sail can be carried.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Loch Carron was 'rather tender' and 'ticklish to handle', often sent down royal yards in port; Loch Broom was 'stiffer' and handled heavy weather differently. Consider these traits when comparing ship records and captain decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perforated sails: placement, size, and operational effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Perforated sails (holes cut into sails) were an innovation meant to reduce the sail 'belly' dead‑wind cushion and to aid in light airs and heavy‑weather handling; hole placement, size and number matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Details: holes 5½–6 inches diameter, roped with grommets; in fore-and-aft sails cut near centre of belly made by the clew; square sails had holes near clews and on line from clews to bunt; topsails/courses generally had four holes; topgallants/royals two holes. Claimed benefits: better close‑hauled performance, less ballooning when running, easier to fur in heavy weather, reduced flogging in calms. Testing method: compare runs with sandbags filling holes and with holes open; use a rag on a stick to detect draught through holes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cargo stowage, trim and stability (safe loading practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper drying and stowage of cargo and maintaining correct trim to avoid top‑heaviness and loss of stability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Loch Carron loaded new, improperly dried rice beneath jute; the rice heated, was re‑stowed into the main hatch and made the vessel top‑heavy, contributing to capsizing events in gales. Inspect cargo moisture, stowage arrangement, and center of gravity when assessing seaworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seamanship and captain's decision‑making
rubrics_metrics.description: Captain and officers' experience, choices (e.g., latitudes chosen, when to sacrifice sails, when to send down masts), and willingness to adopt innovations decisively affect voyage success and speed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Captain Clarke's choices during storms (letting sails go, sacrificing canvass, sending down topgallant masts) saved vessels; Captain Holmes tested perforated sails methodically. Judge voyages with attention to captain competence and tactical decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heavy‑weather tactics and emergency measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques used in severe weather: stripping sails, sacrificing canvas, ceding canvas to save ship, sending down topgallant masts, jury‑rigging and extended tacking to make progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Loch Carron fought gales for 30 days, stripped sails, sent down topgallants, jury‑rigged and tacked for eight days. When evaluating incidents, note the sequence of emergency measures and outcomes (injuries, voyage length, survival).

rubrics_metrics.name: Navigation practice and the necessity of observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Regular celestial/other observations and proper lookout/navigation practice are essential; lack of observations can lead to stranding despite experienced command.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Loss of Lanoma occurred when the captain had 'had no observations for several days' leading to land suddenly appearing at night. Use logs and observation records to audit navigational safety practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crew composition, discipline and human factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality and makeup of the hands (training, discipline, character) affect the ability to work the ship and respond to emergencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Loch Broom's case oil trip from New York involved 'hobos, Bowery toughs and hard cases' who had to be driven to work; such crews create additional operational risk and affect voyage conduct. Consider crew sourcing and discipline when judging voyage difficulty and outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market fit, trade suitability and ship lifecycle
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether a ship's design, capacity and economics match its trade (wool, jute, nitrate, case oil), and recognise lifecycle events such as diversion of trades, sale to foreign owners, and obsolescence due to steam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: many clippers moved from Australian wool trade to Calcutta or nitrate trades; ships were sold to Italians or Norwegians, renamed and repurposed; steam competition forced changes. Evaluate performance in context of trade economics and later sale/repurposing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logging, record‑keeping and documentary evidence of passages
rubrics_metrics.description: Use abstract logs, passage tables, and contemporaneous photographic/official records to substantiate claimed times and events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author cites 'abstract log of Loch Broom’s last voyage' and several tabulated PASSAGES TO AUSTRALIA lists. Treat logs, harbor arrival records and consistent waypoint entries as primary evidence when validating claims.
